paras: The intimidation of Peter Jackson was a series of death threats in November 1888 that drove Jackson, a Black restaurant keeper described as the only Black resident of Bluffton, Wells County, Indiana, out of the county after he voted Republican in the presidential election. According to the Marion Chronicle, three Democrats took a rope to the farmhouse where he was sheltering on the night before the election, meaning to hang him, but the farmer refused to give him up. Republican papers presented the episode as Southern-style "bulldozing" in a Northern state.

Wells County was heavily Democratic, giving a majority of 1,024 on a total vote of 4,854 in 1888. The Chronicle said a Black man had never been allowed to live in Bluffton until Jackson opened a restaurant there; how long he had lived in the town is given variously as months, "a year or two" and ten years. When word spread that he meant to vote Republican, a caucus was held, and he was told he would be "put to death like a dog" if found in town on election day. Jackson himself said several Democrats told him a day or two before the election that they would kill him if he did not vote their ticket.

On the Monday night before the election, on the advice of Republican friends, Jackson went to the home of William McAfee, a farmer several miles from town. The Chronicle named John Deam, Bill High and Dan Puffenbarger as the "Democratic desperadoes" who got a rope and drove to McAfee's house after dark to hang him. McAfee refused to give him up and the men left, while Jackson, by this account, hid in the bushes nearby.

Jackson's own version differed: "two or more Democrats," by his account, came in a buggy, said he was wanted in town, and went back when he appeared with a shotgun; the three accounts all come from interested parties. He did not mention a rope. On election day he voted in Bluffton surrounded by forty or fifty Republicans, and his vote was challenged before it was sworn in. With threats still being made, he left at once for Marion, although a widely reprinted paragraph said the threats were renewed after the election before he was "obliged to leave town."

The Chronicle said the three men would be prosecuted for intimidation. William A. High, a Bluffton grocer, answered in a letter denying that he had gone to McAfee's or sought Jackson, offering $100 to anyone who would swear otherwise, and saying he knew no Dan Poffenberger. He called Jackson "a dead-beat of the first water" and said Jackson had told him in July that he would vote for Cleveland.

By the end of November Jackson was in Indianapolis, where he told a Journal reporter he had come to tell his story to the federal grand jury and would not go back, because Democrats were saying that "not another negro shall ever come into the county." No report of an arrest, indictment or prosecution appears in the coverage.

The Indianapolis Journal carried the Chronicle's story on November 14 under the headline "The Bigoted Bourbons of Wells County Try the Bulldozing Methods of the South." A Journal editorial paragraph the next day said the county's one Black voter had been driven out by "a Democratic mob who tried to kill him" and that there were "counties in Mississippi that couldn't do better than this." The paper also printed High's rebuttal and, on December 1, Jackson's own account under the headline "Driven From His County," ending with his words that "Colored men have never been treated worse in the South than I was there."

Beyond Indiana, the St. Paul Daily Globe ran a short paragraph on November 15 saying Jackson had been "forced by the Democrats to flee to save his neck." The same paragraph appeared in December in the Abilene Weekly Reflector and the Iola Register, and the New-York Tribune printed an Indianapolis special headed "Intimidation in Indiana." The Weekly Courier-Journal of Louisville turned the paragraph around: its Batavia, Ohio, correspondent called it "impudent rot" of Republican sectionalism, in an article on Ohio Republicans driving Black families from schools and townships.

reader.title: Intimidation of Peter Jackson
bases: Jackson was threatened with death to keep him from voting Republican, sought at night at a farmhouse by Democrats (with a rope, per the Chronicle), and forced to leave the county; no one was hurt (A1, A3, A5).

No one was killed or injured; the Chronicle says three men set out to hang Jackson, Jackson speaks of 'two or more', and the stated motive was his Republican vote rather than an accusation of crime (A1, A5).

The Marion Chronicle report and Jackson's own interview agree on the threats, the night visit to the farmer's house, the escorted vote and his flight (A1, A5); William A. High denies only his own part (A4).

accounts.label: Marion Chronicle (via Indianapolis Journal)
accounts.gist: After a caucus threatened Jackson with death, three named Democrats took a rope to McAfee's to hang him; McAfee refused, Jackson hid in the bushes, voted under escort of about forty Republicans and fled to Marion.

accounts.label: Wire/comment paragraph
accounts.gist: Threatened with lynching if he did not vote Democratic, Jackson voted for Harrison; threats were renewed after the election and he had to leave town.

accounts.label: Accused man's letter (William A. High)
accounts.gist: High denies going to McAfee's or seeking Jackson, says he befriended Jackson, calls him a dead-beat, and says Jackson told him he would vote for Cleveland.

accounts.label: Victim's account (Peter Jackson)
accounts.gist: Democrats said they would kill him if he did not vote their ticket; 'two or more' came by buggy to the farmer's house saying he was wanted in town and left when he appeared with a shotgun; his vote was challenged and he fled.

framing.detail: Indianapolis Journal headlines 'The Bigoted Bourbons of Wells County Try the Bulldozing Methods of the South' over a Chronicle text mocking Wells County Democrats as 'negro haters'.
Journal editorial: a 'Democratic mob' tried to kill the county's one colored voter; 'counties in Mississippi that couldn't do better'.
Journal's 'Driven From His County' gives Jackson's own words, ending with the comparison to the South.
St. Paul Globe, Abilene Reflector and Iola Register run the same short paragraph: 'forced by the Democrats to flee to save his neck'.
Courier-Journal's Batavia letter calls the paragraph 'impudent rot' of Republican sectionalism, set against Republican hostility to Black families in Ohio; it does not deny the Indiana facts.
